title: Most Points on One Straight Line
statement:
You get a list of distinct points on a plane, each [x, y] with integer coordinates, for example pins dropped on a map.

Return the largest number of these points that lie on a single straight line. The line can have any direction, including vertical and horizontal.

examples.why: (0, 0), (2, 1) and (4, 2) all lie on y = x / 2. A slope of 0.5 is not an integer, so storing slopes as rounded integers would lose this line.
The three points with x = 5 form a vertical line, whose slope is undefined. Computing dy / dx without care divides by zero there.
Any two points share a line.

hints: Fix one point as an anchor. Every other point defines exactly one line through the anchor. When do two of those lines coincide?
Two points lie on the same line through the anchor exactly when they have the same direction from it. Count directions with a hash map.
Store the direction as a reduced fraction (dy / g, dx / g) with g = gcd, and fix the sign so (1, 2) and (−1, −2) match. That handles vertical lines and avoids floating point.

explain.intuition:
A line is fixed by one point and a direction. So pick each point in turn as the anchor and group every other point by its direction from the anchor. Points with the same direction lie on the same line through the anchor. The biggest group, plus the anchor itself, is the best line through that anchor; the best over all anchors is the answer.

The direction must be a key that compares exactly. A floating slope dy / dx breaks on vertical lines and can round two different slopes to the same number. Instead reduce the vector (dx, dy) by its greatest common divisor and normalize the sign (for example make dx positive, or dy positive when dx is 0). Then (2, 1), (4, 2) and (−2, −1) all become the same key.
steps: If there are at most 2 points, return their count.
For each anchor i, create an empty map of direction → count.
For each later point j: compute dx, dy, divide both by gcd(|dx|, |dy|), and flip both signs if dx < 0, or if dx = 0 and dy < 0.
Increase the count for that key and update best = max(best, count + 1).
pitfalls: Using a floating slope. It divides by zero on vertical lines and is not a safe hash key.
Reducing by the gcd but not normalizing the sign, so the points on opposite sides of the anchor land in different groups.
Forgetting to count the anchor itself (the + 1), or returning 0 for a single point.

complexity.time: O(n² log C) where C bounds the coordinates (for the gcd)

solutions.title: Every pair defines a line, count the rest
solutions.idea: For each pair of points, count how many points are collinear with them using a cross product, which stays exact in integers.

solutions.title: Anchor + reduced direction counts
solutions.idea: For each anchor, group the other points by their gcd-reduced, sign-normalized direction. The biggest group plus the anchor is the best line through it.

followups: Points may now repeat. How do duplicates of the anchor change the count?
Coordinates are floats from a GPS. How would you decide that points are 'on' the same line?
